about: Overview

A financial settlement decides how money, property and other assets are shared when a marriage or civil partnership ends. It can cover the family home, savings, investments, pensions, businesses, debts and ongoing maintenance. In legal terms it is often called a financial remedy, and the final result is a court order.

There is no fixed formula in England and Wales. The law gives the court a wide discretion to reach an outcome that is fair in the circumstances of each family. That flexibility means two couples with similar assets can end up with quite different settlements, depending on their needs, their incomes, the length of the marriage and whether they have children.

Most couples never need a judge to decide. They reach agreement through discussion, solicitor negotiation, mediation or another method, then ask the court to approve it as a consent order. Court proceedings are there for when agreement is not possible, and even then most cases settle before a final hearing.

Without a court order, financial claims between former spouses can stay open, even years after the divorce. A properly made order can bring those claims to an end, so that both people can plan their futures with certainty. For many people, the financial settlement matters far more in the long run than the divorce itself.

People who have been sent a financial statement or court form by their former partner
People who divorced in the past without ever sorting out the finances

How it works

Whether a settlement is agreed or decided by a court, it is built on the same foundations. Each person needs a clear picture of the other's finances, and the outcome has to be one the court would see as fair.

Both people are under a duty to give full and frank disclosure of their finances. This usually means completing a detailed financial statement known as Form E, with supporting documents such as bank statements, payslips, pension valuations, mortgage statements and business accounts. Disclosure continues throughout the process, so significant changes must be shared. Hiding assets can lead to an order being set aside later.

Once both people have the information they need, proposals can be made. This might happen through solicitors, in mediation, in a collaborative meeting or with the help of an arbitrator or private judge. Many settlements are reached at this stage.

If agreement cannot be reached, either person can apply to court, usually after attending a Mediation Information and Assessment Meeting unless an exemption applies. Court cases generally follow three stages.

list: A first appointment, where the judge identifies the issues and decides what further information or valuations are needed
A financial dispute resolution appointment, where a judge gives an indication of the likely outcome to help both people settle
A final hearing, where a different judge hears evidence and makes a decision

about: The courts now expect people to give serious thought to resolving things outside court, and a judge can pause a case to encourage this. Many cases settle at or soon after the financial dispute resolution appointment.

about.h3: Turning the agreement into an order

about: However the agreement is reached, it is usually set out in a consent order, which the court is asked to approve. A consent order can only be approved once the conditional order in the divorce has been made. Some parts, such as a pension share, only take effect once the final order is made.

about.h3: Money while the case is ongoing

about: Settlements can take time, and bills still need paying in the meantime. Some couples agree temporary arrangements for the mortgage, household bills and maintenance while they negotiate. If that is not possible, the court can make an interim maintenance order to cover essential needs until the final order. A solicitor can explain whether this might be needed.

A settlement reached soon after disclosure can sometimes be approved within a few months. Cases that go through all the court stages can take a year or more. The speed often depends on how quickly both people provide information and how far apart their positions are.
What the court considers

When deciding what is fair, the court looks at a list of factors set out in law. It gives first consideration to the welfare of any children of the family under 18. It then weighs up the full circumstances of the case. Your solicitor will explain how these factors are likely to apply to you.

list: The income, earning capacity, property and other resources each person has or is likely to have
The financial needs, obligations and responsibilities each person has or is likely to have
The standard of living the family enjoyed before the breakdown of the marriage
The age of each person and the length of the marriage
Any physical or mental disability
The contributions each person has made, including looking after the home and caring for the family
Conduct, but only in rare cases where it would be unfair to ignore it
Benefits either person will lose because of the divorce, such as pension rights

about: In practice, courts often think about three ideas. Needs, especially housing for both people and any children, usually come first, and in many cases the available assets are only enough to meet needs. Sharing reflects the idea that wealth built up during the marriage is a joint effort, and equal division is often a starting point in that context, though not a rule. Compensation is rarely used, but can apply where one person gave up a career for the family.

about.h3: Assets from before the marriage or from family

about: Assets brought into the marriage, inherited or received as gifts may be treated differently from those built up together. Whether they are shared depends on how they have been used, how long ago they were received and whether they are needed to meet either person's needs. This is often an area where advice is especially useful.

The court must consider whether a clean break is possible, so that former spouses have no ongoing financial ties. Where one person cannot meet their needs without support, maintenance may be ordered instead, for a fixed period or sometimes longer.
Home and pensions
For many families the two most valuable assets are the home and the pensions. They are often dealt with together, and there are several ways of dividing them.

Options for the home usually include selling it and dividing the proceeds, one person buying out the other, or one person staying in the home for a period before it is sold. The last option is sometimes used to give children a stable home until they finish school. Mortgage capacity, the cost of rehousing both people and the needs of the children are all important. A solicitor can explain the options that might work for your family.
Pensions can be worth far more than people expect, and their value is not always obvious from a statement. There are three main ways of dealing with them.

list: Pension sharing, where a percentage of one pension is transferred to the other person to create their own pension
Offsetting, where one person keeps more of the pension and the other keeps more of another asset, such as the home
Pension attachment, where part of a pension is paid to the other person when it comes into payment

about: Different types of pension, such as public sector schemes and private defined contribution pots, can work very differently. In some cases a specialist pension report is obtained to help compare options. Your solicitor will explain whether this is needed.

If either person owns a business, it may need to be valued, and the court will think about how much money can be taken out of it without harming it. Business owners often ask for advice early, as valuations can take time.

Debts are part of the picture too. Joint debts, such as a mortgage or loan, usually remain the responsibility of both people as far as the lender is concerned, whatever the court orders between the couple. Your solicitor can explain how debts are usually taken into account.

Bank accounts, shares, ISAs, cryptocurrency, cars, valuable possessions and money owed to either person can all form part of the settlement. Everything needs to be disclosed, even if one person believes it should be kept out of the pot. Your solicitor will explain how different types of asset are usually treated.

Transferring property or investments between former spouses can have tax consequences, for example capital gains tax on a second property or shares. The rules on tax change, so many solicitors suggest checking the position with an accountant before an agreement is finalised.
Costs

The cost of a financial settlement depends mainly on how quickly agreement is reached and how complex the assets are. A simple case that settles after disclosure costs far less than one that goes to a final hearing.

Financial work is usually charged by the hour, or in stages with an estimate for each one, such as disclosure, negotiation, and each court hearing. Some firms offer a fixed fee for particular stages, or for preparing for and attending a financial dispute resolution appointment. Ask the firm to explain their approach in writing.

list: The court fee for a financial application or for approval of a consent order
Valuations of property, businesses or pensions
Mediation, arbitration or private judge fees if those routes are used
Barristers' fees if a case goes to a hearing

about: Court fees change from time to time, so check GOV.UK or ask the firm. If you have a low income, you may be able to get help with court fees.

about.h3: If one person controls the money

about: Where one person has much more access to money than the other, the court can order them to pay towards the other's legal fees so that both can be fairly represented. A solicitor can explain whether this might apply.

In financial cases the general rule is that each person pays their own costs. The court can depart from this if someone behaves unreasonably, for example by refusing to give proper disclosure or by not negotiating openly.

Common problems
Financial settlements can be stressful, especially when trust has broken down. These are some of the issues that often arise.

Delays are often caused by one person not providing documents, or providing them slowly. The court can order disclosure and can draw conclusions from a failure to provide it. If you think assets are being hidden, tell your solicitor.
If someone is trying to move or dispose of assets to defeat a claim, the court can sometimes make orders to stop it or reverse it. Act quickly and speak to a solicitor if you are concerned.
Some people agree to a settlement just to get things over with, without fully understanding pensions or other assets. Taking advice before you agree can help you understand what you are giving up.

Some people have been controlled financially by a partner, for example by being kept from money or forced into debt. This can be a form of domestic abuse. If you are at risk, contact the police on 999 in an emergency or a domestic abuse support service. A solicitor can explain how the court deals with these situations.

Capital orders, such as property transfers and lump sums, are usually final. Maintenance orders can usually be varied if circumstances change. In rare cases an order can be set aside, for example where there was serious non disclosure or a major unforeseen event soon after. These are complex areas where advice is essential.
faqs: The basics
Is everything split 50 50?

Not automatically. The court looks at a range of factors, including needs, resources, contributions and the length of the marriage. Equal sharing of assets built up during the marriage is often a starting point, but needs, especially housing for children, frequently lead to a different split. A solicitor can explain how this works in your situation.
Do we need a court order if we agree?

An agreement is not legally binding on its own. To make it binding and close off future claims, it is usually turned into a consent order approved by the court. Without one, claims can remain open for years, even after the divorce is final. The order also gives both people a clear way to enforce the terms if they are not followed.
When should we sort out finances?

Many couples start during the divorce, often in the 20 week reflection period. A consent order cannot be approved until the conditional order has been made. Solicitors often discuss delaying the final order until the financial order is in place, to protect certain rights. Starting early can also make the separation feel more settled for everyone.
What if we divorced years ago without a financial order?

Financial claims can stay open after divorce unless a court order has dealt with them. A former spouse may still be able to apply, although delay is one of the things the court takes into account. If you remarried before making a claim, your own claims may be limited. A solicitor can explain your position.
Does it matter whose name things are in?

Less than many people think. In a divorce, the court can look at assets held by either spouse, whether they are in joint names or one name. Legal ownership is still relevant, but it does not decide how assets will be divided. Assets held by companies or trusts can also be relevant. A solicitor can explain how ownership affects your case.
Does the reason for the divorce affect the money?

Usually not. The court only takes conduct into account in rare cases where it would be unfair to ignore it, such as serious financial misconduct. Most of the time, who was to blame for the breakdown makes no difference to the settlement. Under no fault divorce, the reasons for the breakdown are not part of the divorce application either.
Are unmarried couples treated the same way?

No. Unmarried couples do not have the same financial claims when they separate, however long they lived together. Disputes about a shared home are usually decided under property law. There may be claims for the benefit of children. A solicitor can explain the difference. This is why some couples who live together choose to make a cohabitation agreement.
Can we agree a settlement without solicitors?

Some couples do reach agreement themselves, sometimes with a mediator. To become legally binding, the agreement still needs to be turned into a consent order and approved by the court. Many people ask a solicitor to check the agreement and draft the order, so that it does what they intend.
Disclosure and information
What is Form E?

Form E is the standard financial statement used in financial cases in England and Wales. It sets out your income, assets, debts, pensions and needs, with supporting documents. It is used in court proceedings and is often used voluntarily in negotiation too, so that both people have the same information.
What documents will I need?

Typically twelve months of bank statements, recent payslips or tax returns, pension valuations, mortgage statements, details of savings and investments, and business accounts if you have a business. Your solicitor will give you a checklist. Gathering documents early can save time and costs. If you do not have access to some documents, such as joint account statements, tell your solicitor, as there are ways of obtaining them.
What if my ex will not give full disclosure?

The court can order disclosure, and can draw conclusions about someone's finances if they fail to provide it. Costs orders can also be made against people who do not cooperate. Your solicitor can explain the options for obtaining the information. In serious cases, a settlement reached without full disclosure can later be set aside. Keep a note of anything you think is missing and share it with your solicitor.
Can I look at my partner's private documents?

Be careful. Taking or copying documents that belong to your partner, or accessing their emails or accounts without permission, can be unlawful and can harm your case. Tell your solicitor what you know or suspect, and they will explain the proper ways to obtain information. Documents you already have lawful access to, such as joint statements, are different.
What is a pension report?

In some cases a specialist actuary is asked to prepare a report comparing the value of pensions and suggesting how they might be shared fairly. These reports are often useful where pensions are large or of different types. Your solicitor will explain whether one is likely to be needed. The cost is often shared between both people.
Do I have to disclose money I have received since we separated?

Yes. Disclosure covers your current finances, not just those at the date of separation. New income, an inheritance or a change of job all need to be disclosed, and the duty continues until the case ends. Your solicitor will explain how assets acquired after separation are usually treated. Failing to disclose can be costly later.
Home, pensions and assets
Can I stay in the family home?

It depends on the assets available, both people's housing needs, and the needs of any children. Options include one person buying the other out, or staying in the home for a period before it is sold. A solicitor can explain what might be realistic in your circumstances. Mortgage capacity and the cost of rehousing are often key.
Are pensions included?

Yes. Pensions are often one of the most valuable assets, and can be shared, offset against other assets or attached. Pensions built up before the marriage may be treated differently from those built up during it. Your solicitor will explain the options. Pensions are sometimes overlooked because their value is not obvious, so make sure you have up to date valuations before any agreement is reached.
Is an inheritance protected?

Not always. Inherited money and assets may be treated differently from assets built up together, but they can still be shared if they are needed to meet either person's needs or have been mixed with family money. How an inheritance is treated depends on the facts of each case. Expected future inheritances are usually treated differently.
What happens to my business?

A business may need to be valued, and the court will consider how much can be taken from it without harming it. Options include one person keeping the business and the other receiving other assets. Your solicitor will explain how business assets are usually dealt with. Valuations can take time, so it helps to start early. Shares in a family business, partnerships and farms can raise particular issues.
What happens to joint debts?

Joint debts, such as a mortgage or loan, usually remain the responsibility of both people as far as the lender is concerned. A settlement can decide who repays what between you, but it does not change the agreement with the lender unless the lender agrees. It can help to tell lenders about the separation and keep paying while things are resolved, to protect both credit records.
What about savings or property abroad?

Assets abroad are still part of the financial picture and must be disclosed. Enforcing an order over property in another country can be more complicated. A solicitor with international experience can explain how these assets are usually dealt with. The court can still take them into account, and can make orders against a person in England and Wales even if the property is overseas. Valuations and currency changes may need to be considered.
Can I keep my pension if my spouse keeps the house?

This is called offsetting, and it is a common way of dealing with pensions. It can work well, but comparing a pension with a share of a house is not straightforward, because they are very different kinds of asset. A solicitor, and sometimes a pension expert, can help you understand what you would be giving up.
Maintenance
What is spousal maintenance?

It is regular payments from one former spouse to the other to help meet their income needs. It may be ordered for a fixed period or, less commonly, for longer. The court will consider whether the receiving person can adjust to independence over time. How much is paid depends on needs, income and earning capacity. It is not paid automatically, and in many cases there is a clean break instead.
How is child maintenance dealt with?

Child maintenance is usually arranged between parents or through the Child Maintenance Service, which uses a set formula. In some cases child maintenance can be included in a court order by agreement. Your solicitor can explain how it fits alongside a financial settlement. Child maintenance is separate from time with the children, and one does not depend on the other.
Can maintenance be changed later?

Usually yes. Maintenance orders can generally be varied if either person's circumstances change significantly. Some orders include terms that prevent the length being extended. Maintenance for a former spouse normally ends if they remarry. Changes are usually made by agreement or by applying to the court, and the court looks at all the circumstances, including any change in income, health or living arrangements. A solicitor can explain whether a variation might be possible.
What is a clean break?

A clean break means former spouses have no ongoing financial claims against each other once the order is carried out. The court must consider whether a clean break is possible. It is not always suitable, for example where one person cannot meet their needs without support. Where maintenance is needed, a clean break may still be possible later, once the maintenance term ends.
Can I get money to live on before the case ends?

Yes, in some cases. If agreement cannot be reached about temporary support, the court can order interim maintenance to cover essential needs until the case is finished. A solicitor can explain whether this might be appropriate and how it is applied for. Temporary arrangements can often be agreed without going to court.
Court and costs
How long does a financial case take?

If agreement is reached early, a settlement can sometimes be finalised in a few months. Cases that go through court can take a year or more, depending on complexity and court availability. Your solicitor will give you an idea once they understand your situation. Delays in disclosure and valuations are common causes of longer cases.
What happens at a financial dispute resolution appointment?

It is a hearing where both people and their lawyers set out their positions, and a judge gives an indication of the likely outcome. The aim is to help both people settle. What is said is confidential, and the same judge does not decide the case at a final hearing.
Do I have to try mediation before going to court?

You usually need to attend a Mediation Information and Assessment Meeting before applying, unless an exemption applies, such as evidence of domestic abuse. The courts expect people to consider ways of settling outside court and can pause cases to encourage it. Mediation may not be suitable where there has been domestic abuse, and a solicitor can explain other options.
How much will a financial settlement cost?

It depends on how complex the finances are and how quickly agreement is reached. Most firms charge by the hour or in stages, and there may be court fees and valuation costs. Ask for a written estimate. Leaflegal is free to use, and the firm pays us for the introduction.
What if my ex is moving money to defeat my claim?

The court can sometimes make orders to stop assets being moved or to reverse transactions made to defeat a claim. It is important to act quickly. Speak to a solicitor as soon as you are concerned. Keep a record of anything you notice, such as large withdrawals, property being put up for sale or assets being transferred to friends or family, and share it with your solicitor.
What will the solicitor ask me?

Expect questions about your marriage, children, home, income, savings, pensions, debts and what you would like to happen. Have a rough list of assets and debts ready, along with any court papers. You do not need exact figures at the first conversation. They will also ask whether there are any safety concerns.
